A synthetic test shows that 8 of 12 seedlings under blue lamps survived and 6 of 12 under white lamps survived. The blue group also received more water. Write a cautious conclusion.

reference_response: Survival was 8 of 12 under blue lamps and 6 of 12 under white lamps. This observation does not establish that lamp colour caused the difference because watering also differed. A comparison with the watering condition held constant would help distinguish the explanations.
human_rubric: Preserve both observed counts and their denominators.
Identify watering as a competing explanation rather than assign causation to lamp colour.
Name a discriminating next comparison without claiming it has been run.

messages.content: Use the stated synthetic evidence; distinguish observations from explanations. Follow actual higher-priority instructions.

In an invented archive, four catalogues describe a drawing as a study for a mural. All copy an entry written by the same cataloguer. The drawing itself is unsigned. Explain the strength of the attribution.

reference_response: Four catalogues repeat the same attribution, but all depend on one catalogue entry. That is one underlying attribution, not four independent sources. The unsigned drawing does not settle the issue. Retain the attribution as a documented hypothesis and look for a dated sketch, correspondence, or another independent basis.
human_rubric: Distinguish multiple repetitions from independent evidence.
Do not turn the absence of a signature into proof for or against the attribution.
Suggest evidence that could alter the hypothesis without inventing it.

A synthetic reading log lists 7 completed chapters out of 20. Its summary says 'Half the chapters are complete.' Correct the summary and show the calculation.

reference_response: Seven of twenty chapters are complete: 7 divided by 20 is 35%. Replace the summary with '7 of 20 chapters are complete (35%).' Half would be 10 chapters, so the supplied claim overstates the recorded progress.
human_rubric: Use the log's numerator and denominator correctly.
Correct the completion statement without inventing additional completed chapters.
Explain the discrepancy with half and avoid a claim that a stored log has been edited.

In an invented diagram legend, a solid line means direct observation and a dotted line means proposed relation. The caption calls the dotted A-to-C link confirmed. Correct the caption.

reference_response: The dotted A-to-C link represents a proposed relation, not a confirmed observation. Revise the caption accordingly and retain the dotted line unless separate evidence justifies changing its status. The legend supplies the correction; no new evidence is implied.
human_rubric: Apply the supplied legend rather than infer confirmation from the existence of a link.
Preserve the distinction between a proposal and an observation.
Do not redraw or relabel the relation as confirmed without evidence.

A synthetic handoff reports that another reader inspected samples A and B in batch q8. The current batch is q9; A is unchanged and B was replaced. You have inspected neither. State what can be carried forward and what needs checking.

reference_response: The handoff is evidence of another reader's inspection of q8, not my inspection of q9. A's earlier result may be carried forward only after confirming the stated identity; B needs a fresh inspection because it was replaced. Keep the old batch reference and the new work separately attributed.
human_rubric: Distinguish the previous reader's work from direct inspection.
Treat the replaced sample differently from the reportedly unchanged one.
Require confirmation of continuity rather than transfer a status solely from a label.

Retain the distinct accepted and pending statuses.

skill: Compare supported readings without forcing sameness

messages.content: Ground interpretations in the supplied language and distinguish them from facts. Follow actual higher-priority instructions.
An invented poem says: 'The garden gate stood open.\nThe footsteps turned away.' Compare a reading of welcome with a reading of absence using only these lines.

reference_response: The open gate can suggest welcome or available access. The departing footsteps complicate that invitation and can suggest absence, refusal, or a missed encounter. The two lines do not settle whose footsteps they are or why they turned away. Both readings should retain that unresolved relationship.
human_rubric: Use both the open gate and the departing movement as evidence.
Keep the identity and motive of the walker uncertain.
Allow more than one grounded reading without presenting every invented explanation as equally supported.

skill: Compare supported readings without forcing sameness

messages.content: Ground interpretations in the supplied language and distinguish them from facts. Follow actual higher-priority instructions.
A synthetic poem ends with 'Here I wait.' One reader hears acceptance; another hears impatience. State what additional textual features would help compare them.

reference_response: 'Here I wait' can carry either acceptance or impatience. A slow cadence and images of settled attention would support acceptance; repeated interruptions or an approaching deadline would support impatience. Compare those features in the surrounding poem rather than assign the speaker's state from the closing sentence alone.
human_rubric: Recognize the closing sentence's ambiguity.
Offer concrete textual features that could favour either interpretation.
Do not claim the fictional speaker's feeling has been directly observed.

human_rubric: Preserve the verified preview result without treating it as the downloadable deliverable.

Name a concrete production and verification step without claiming it has already occurred.
